2NF (Strict key dependencies): require 1NF
No non-prime (not part of candidate key) attribute Y dpeends on a subset Z \sub X of a candidate key X
e.g.
NOT FULFILL: (Candidate key: {ISBN, AuthorId}, AuthorId -> AuthorName)
(ISBN, AuthorId, Author name), (423423453, 3433, Elmari), (423423453, 5522, Navathe)

3NF (Decomposition (lossless) of transitive FDs): require 2NF
All non-prime attributes Y are defined by a candidate key/prime key

Atomicity : "all or none"
If a database crashes or fails to execute completely all transaction commands then we end up in an inconsistent state (e.g., lost 100)
The atomicity property promises that either:
- All transaction commands are executed
- None of the transaction commands is executed.
(In both cases the sum of the two accounts is 1100sek)

Durability: "all updates are persisted"
Committing/Completing a transaction should ensure that the state updates are preserved!
Database Systems ensure durability by precommitting state or updates (write ahead log) on non-volatile storage-before saying “done”, in a recoverable manner.

Concurrent equivalent:
- Two schedules with the same operations are equivalent if respective read and therefore, write operations have the same values.
- Two equivalent schedules lead to the same database instance (state).
- A schedule that has an equivalent serial schedule is called serialisable

Conflicting operations: (r(Q), w(Q)), (w(Q), r(Q))
o_i, o_j \in S \conflicting:
- originate from different transactions (o_i \in T_i, o_j \in T_j, T_i!=T_j)
- access same object Q
- At least one write (o_i = w(Q) \or o_j = w(Q))

Conflict equivalent schedules
<-> same set of transaction operations, conflicting operations match and have the same order
